title: Effects of realistic pulse shapes in two-dimensional spectroscopy
authors: M. Russo, R. Gilliot, A. Blech, M. Joffre, C. P. Koch, H. Seiler
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) spectroscopy is a powerful pump-pump-probe technique for revealing couplings between quantum states and disentangling the different contributions to the optical response of a system. We present an efficient method for 2D spectroscopy simulations in the Markovian limit for the environment, capable of handling arbitrary pulse shapes and reproducing time-ordering and overlapping pulse effects, while maintaining a computational cost that scales linearly with the number of sampling points. We leverage this framework to investigate how 2D spectra are affected by spectral phase distortions and highly non-Gaussian pulse shapes, such as those produced experimentally by hollow-core fibers or non-collinear optical amplifiers. We show that realistic pulses can induce the appearance of additional spectral features, lineshape distortions and oscillating contributions in the system's dynamics. Notably, even weak temporal pulse tails arising from uncorrected high-order spectral phase terms cause visible changes in the 2D spectra. We also find that homodyne detection schemes employed in experiments can mitigate the presence of such pulse effects. These results emphasize the importance of including realistic pulses in 2D spectroscopy simulations to identify pulse-induced effects and minimize ambiguities in the interpretation of experimental data.
summary: This paper presents an advanced theoretical method to simulate 2D spectroscopy signals by accurately incorporating the effects of realistic, non-ideal laser pulses. The authors demonstrate that neglecting these pulse characteristics leads to incorrect interpretations of quantum dynamics. By achieving linear scaling, they provide a powerful tool for interpreting complex experimental data in AMO physics.
main_problem: To accurately simulate Two-dimensional (2D) spectroscopy by accounting for the effects of realistic pulse shapes, spectral phase distortions, and temporal pulse tails.
main_result: Realistic pulses induce additional spectral features, lineshape distortions, and oscillating contributions in 2D spectra, emphasizing that simulations must incorporate these effects for correct data interpretation.
method: The authors developed an efficient simulation method by recasting the computationally intensive triple convolution integral into a form allowing linear scaling with sampling points under the Markovian approximation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on 2D spectroscopy, a pump-pump-probe technique used to probe quantum state couplings. Models include anharmonic oscillators and two-exciton systems.
key_observables: The 2D spectrum $E^{(3)}_S(	au, T, t)$, spectral features, lineshape distortions, and oscillating contributions in the system's dynamics.
important_parameters: Pulse shapes (Gaussian, chirped, double/triple-peaked), time delays ($	au, T$), and pulse overlap effects.
main_assumptions: The primary simplification relies on the Markovian assumption for the environment. The Rotating Wave Approximation (RWA) is also used.
figures_summary: Figures compare 2D spectra under various pulse shapes (IL vs. TL vs. CH) for two-exciton and dimer systems, showing how spectral features change with pulse complexity.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the theoretical framework to calculate the signal $E^{(3)}_S$ by separating contributions into partial response functions ($R_j$) and integral terms ($I_{j,\sigma}$), followed by applying this method to model various physical systems under different realistic excitation conditions.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a computationally tractable framework for simulating complex quantum optical measurements, directly addressing how experimental artifacts (like pulse shape imperfections) manifest in fundamental spectroscopic observables.
